newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FEATURE - Dutch sweet addicts abroad get their fix.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Dutch sweet addicts abroad get their fix.

text.p: Born of a father's concern for his homesick offspring abroad, the Dutch Drop of the Month Club now satisfies the cravings of 2,300 liquorice-lovers all over the globe.
Usually black and frequently sticky, liquorice's charms leave most people unaffected except for the Dutch and the Scandinavians who are massively addicted to it.

Frank Fehmers started the club 18 months ago as a way of dispatching the black booty to desperate members of his family and their friends living abroad, formalising an ad hoc arrangement as demand spiralled out of control.
"It was madness, he just couldn't keep up with demand," said Drop of the Month Club spokesman Rolf Boost in an interview.

According to the Dutch confectionery sector-magazine Consudel, the country's 15 million inhabitants annually feast on more than 15 million kilos (16,500 tons) of liquorice worth a total of 130 million guilders ($69 million).

The "drop" or liquorice market continues to swell, adding around five percent last year, according to Consudel, as the Dutch clamour for twists, spirals, bullets, coins, cats, bears, beehives, straps and double salted cubes made from the delicacy.

"Market research has established (that) over half of the Dutch eat liquorice. In most countries, the stuff is unavailable. Which means some 325,000 Dutch abroad miss out. But this is no longer necessary," said Boost.
LIQUORICE POSTED ALL OVER WORLD
Drop lovers can be found in countries all over the world such as South Africa, China and El Salvador. Closer to home Belgium and Spain are among the destinations for liquorice mercy missions.
Every month, the Club's members receive a big envelope carrying one carefully selected kilo (2.2 lb) of the 15 most popular liquorice varieties.
"The drop-packages should be resistant to climatic changes, and also have to comply with general customs criteria and country-specific rules on the ingredients," said Boost.
Although the range broadly remains the same throughout the year, sometimes, there's a special treat.
"For Christmas, we included an extra roll of peppermints," said Boost, adding that members appreciated the initiative.
One kilo a month of liquorice may seem a lot to the layman, but it comes down to a modest dose of eight "dropjes" a day, not always sufficient for the connoisseurs.
"We have members receiving four kilos a month," said Boost, adding these were often families.
The cherished kilos are wrapped in three smaller packages in order to avoid rows.
"Otherwise dad might take the whole lot with him into his office, leaving the rest of the household with empty hands," explains Boost.
CLUB LETTER KEEPS SUBSCRIBERS POSTED
A newsletter relating how things fare within the Club, narrating special events and detailing the unexpected routes some dropjes take, accompanies every sticky portion.

"We are a club of friends really, not a business. Members write to us about how they feel, saying what's happening to them and to their drop. We intend to issue an annual club magazine, recapitulating the members' mail," said Boost.
When the Club's eight enthusiasts decided to publish advertisements in a couple of Dutch-language magazines throughout the world last spring, they were unaware of the scale of expatriate demand.
"Drop lovers used to gradually turn to us by word of mouth. But with the ads, we got buried in an avalanche of demand," said Boost.
He added that advertisements published during the Christmas season in Dutch newspapers -- "do you know any drop-addicts abroad?" -- had caused a renewed wave of interest.
"There are hundreds of them. We're still counting the letters," Boost said.
BRIGHT FUTURE SEEN
Boost, who said he was absolutely not a liquorice-lover but was delighted to collect the often exotic stamps on the members' mail, said he spent about one hour each day on the club.
"We (the eight volunteers) all have our occupations in the 'real world'. The craze about the club took us more or less off guard but it's definitely a lot of fun," he said.
He predicts a bright future for the Club.

"I think we'll have over three thousand members this year. Maybe we'll get to 10,000 or 20,000 members, then we'll have to hire somebody. But we don't want this to turn into a commercial business, we want to keep the club feeling," he said.
($ = 1.892 Dutch Guilders)
